title: Once more (Judges 16:28–30)
hookLine: blind and chained, Samson prays for strength one last time

cards: A prison house in Gaza. The Philistines have put out Samson's eyes, bound him in bronze chains, and set him to grind.
The man who once tore a young lion apart with his bare hands now grinds grain for the people who blinded him.
Then, almost in passing, the text drops in one sentence: "Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven." Nobody in the prison notices. The reader does.

teach.b: The lords of the Philistines gather for a great feast to their god Dagon, and send for Samson to entertain them. The house is packed; people crowd the roof to watch.
A boy leads him in by the hand, and Samson asks him something small: let me feel the pillars the house stands on, so I can lean on them. Then he prays.

"O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God." It isn't the first time he has called on God; once, dying of thirst after a battle, he cried out and water came.
But through all the lions and snapped ropes, the text never shows him asking for strength. Now, blind and weak, he does. Remember me.
Only this once. The text doesn't clean up his prayer, either. He asks to be avenged for his two eyes.
The Mishnah says Samson went after his eyes, following what he saw and wanted, and so it was his eyes the Philistines took.

The tradition keeps both truths: a man whose own choices brought him here, and a God who still hears him when he asks. He braces against the two middle pillars, and the house comes down, and he dies with them.
He asked, and at the end, the strength came.

how: Jews read Samson's death in Judges 16 as part of the Former Prophets, often with the Mishnah's comment that Samson 'went after his eyes' beside the text.

s: the text says Samson's hair began to grow again in prison
one quiet sentence, before the feast: the hair of his head began to grow again.
Samson had never called on God before this prayer
once before, thirsty after a battle, he cried out and water came.
the text hides Samson's wish for revenge
his prayer asks to be avenged for his two eyes; the text keeps it as he said it.

games.q: you're Samson, blind, brought out to entertain a crowd. a boy holds your hand. what do you ask him?
o: take me back to the prison.
let me feel the pillars, so I can lean on them.
games.why: he asks to feel the pillars, then prays: remember me, and strengthen me only this once.

practice: If there's a place where you're worn down right now, name it without dressing it up. Then, like Samson reaching for the pillars, lean on something, the chair under you, the floor, your own breath, and rest your weight there.
If you pray, borrow two of his words, remember me; if you don't, let yourself want strength without being ashamed of wanting it.

wordCard.voice: Once more. Samson's last prayer, blind and chained in Gaza: remember me, and strengthen me only this once.

orig.note: Hebrew: this time, once; Samson asks for strength 'only this once' in Judges 16:28.

carryVoice: Your line: only this once. Even at the bottom, he could still ask. Day seven hundred twenty-five.
